reminder: A bilinear form takes two vectors to a scalar and is linear in each argument.
definition: A bilinear form on a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over a field $K$ is a map $B:V\times V\to K$ that is a [linear map](c:linear-map) in each argument when the other argument is fixed. That is, $B(au+bv,w)=aB(u,w)+bB(v,w)$ and $B(w,au+bv)=aB(w,u)+bB(w,v)$.
examples: The dot product $B(x,y)=\sum_i x_iy_i$ on $\mathbb R^n$.
For every $n\times n$ matrix $A$, the map $B(x,y)=x^{T}Ay$ on $K^n$.
The determinant $B(x,y)=x_1y_2-x_2y_1$ of two vectors in $\mathbb R^2$.
Non-example: $B(x,y)=x+y$ on $\mathbb R$ is not bilinear, because $B(2x,y)=2x+y$ is not equal to $2B(x,y)$.

steps: A bilinear map $V\times W\to U$ is linear in each argument when the other argument is fixed.
Take $W=V$ and let $U=K$ be the field of scalars.
The resulting map $B:V\times V\to K$ is a bilinear form.
So the form adds that both arguments lie in one space and that the value is a scalar.
links.why: A form is the scalar-valued case of a bilinear map, so results on bilinear maps apply to it.

reminder: A countable set has a one-to-one map into the natural numbers.
definition: A set $S$ is countable when there is a [bijection](c:bijection) from $S$ onto a subset of the [natural numbers](c:natural-number). Equivalently, $S$ is empty or there is a surjection $\mathbb N\to S$. Finite sets count as countable.
examples: Every finite set, and also $\mathbb N$, $\mathbb Z$ and $\mathbb Q$.
The set of all finite words over a finite alphabet.
Non-example: $\mathbb R$ is not countable, because Cantor's diagonal argument gives a real number outside every list.

steps: Take a finite set $S$ with $n$ elements.
List its elements as $s_1,\dots,s_n$ and send $s_i$ to $i$.
This map is a bijection from $S$ onto $\{1,\dots,n\}$, a subset of the natural numbers.
So $S$ is countable, and countable sets also include infinite ones such as $\mathbb N$.
links.why: Every result about countable sets covers finite sets too, and the infinite case is the new content.

reminder: A formal power series is an infinite sum $\sum a_nx^n$ with ring coefficients, and it needs no convergence.
definition: A formal power series over a [ring](c:ring) $R$ is a sequence $(a_n)_{n\ge0}$ in $R$, written $\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n$. Series add coefficientwise and multiply like [polynomials](c:polynomial), by $\left(\sum a_nx^n\right)\left(\sum b_nx^n\right)=\sum_n\left(\sum_{i+j=n}a_ib_j\right)x^n$, so no limit is ever taken.
examples: $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n$ is the inverse of $1-x$ in the ring $\mathbb Z[[x]]$.
Every polynomial is a formal power series with finitely many nonzero coefficients.
Non-example: $\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}x^n$ is not a formal power series, because it has negative powers and the coefficient of $x^0$ in its square is an infinite sum.

steps: Take a polynomial $a_0+a_1x+\dots+a_dx^d$ over $R$.
Set $a_n=0$ for every $n>d$.
The coefficient sequence $(a_n)$ is then a formal power series.
Sums and products of polynomials agree with those of series, so polynomials sit inside power series.
links.why: Power series extend polynomial algebra to infinite sums, and a polynomial is a series with finite support.

reminder: A graph coloring gives every vertex a color so that adjacent vertices get different colors.
definition: A coloring of a [graph](c:graph) $G=(V,E)$ with a set $C$ of colors is a map $c:V\to C$ such that $c(u)\ne c(v)$ whenever $\{u,v\}$ is an edge of $G$. It is a $k$-coloring when $C$ has $k$ elements.
examples: A path on three vertices has a 2-coloring: color the vertices red, blue, red.
An odd cycle, such as a triangle, has a 3-coloring but no 2-coloring.
Non-example: giving the three vertices of a triangle only two colors fails, because two vertices share a color and are adjacent.

reminder: A Hamiltonian is the energy function of a phase space, and its vector field gives the time evolution.
definition: On a [Poisson manifold](c:poisson-manifold) $(X,\{\cdot,\cdot\})$, a Hamiltonian is a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $H:X\to\mathbb R$, read as the energy. Its [Hamiltonian vector field](c:hamiltonian-vector-field), the [derivation](c:derivation) $f\mapsto\{f,H\}$, generates the time evolution $\dot f=\{f,H\}$. In quantum mechanics a self-adjoint operator plays this role.
examples: A particle on a line, with phase space $\mathbb R^2$, bracket $\{q,p\}=1$ and $H=\tfrac12p^2+V(q)$.
The harmonic oscillator $H=\tfrac12(p^2+q^2)$, whose flow turns the phase plane in circles.
Non-example: the operator $\nabla$ of vector analysis, which some authors call a Hamilton operator, is unrelated and is not an energy function.

reminder: An immersion is a smooth map whose differential is injective at every point.
definition: A smooth map $f:M\to N$ between [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) is an immersion when, for every $p\in M$, the differential $df_p:T_pM\to T_{f(p)}N$ between [tangent spaces](c:tangent-space) is an [injection](c:injection). Equivalently, near each point $f$ looks like the inclusion $\mathbb R^m\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^n$ in suitable charts.
examples: The inclusion of the circle $S^1$ into $\mathbb R^2$.
The figure-eight curve $t\mapsto(\sin 2t,\sin t)$ is an immersion of $S^1$ into $\mathbb R^2$ that is not injective.
Non-example: $t\mapsto(t^2,t^3)$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R^2$ is not an immersion, because its derivative is zero at $t=0$.

steps: Take a smooth embedding $f:M\to N$, a smooth map that is a homeomorphism onto its image.
Its differential is injective at every point, as part of the definition of a smooth embedding.
So $f$ is an immersion.
An immersion may drop the condition that $f$ is a homeomorphism onto its image, so it may cross itself.
links.why: Immersions are the local version of embeddings, so a theorem about immersions covers every embedding.

reminder: An injection sends different inputs to different outputs.
definition: A [function](c:function) $f:A\to B$ is an injection when $f(a)=f(a')$ implies $a=a'$ for all $a,a'\in A$. For nonempty $A$, this is equivalent to $f$ having a left inverse $g:B\to A$ with $g\circ f=\mathrm{id}_A$.
examples: The map $x\mapsto2x+1$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R$.
The inclusion of a subset $A\subseteq B$ into $B$.
Non-example: $x\mapsto x^2$ on $\mathbb R$ is not an injection, because $f(-1)=f(1)$.

steps: Take a bijection $f:A\to B$.
By definition $f$ is both injective and surjective.
Drop the condition that $f$ is surjective.
What remains is an injection, so every bijection is an injection and the converse fails.
links.why: A bijection is an injection onto the whole target, so injection facts apply to every bijection.

reminder: A Jordan curve is the image of a continuous one-to-one map from the circle.
definition: A Jordan curve in a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is a subset $C\subseteq X$ that is the image of a [continuous](c:continuous-function) [injection](c:injection) $\gamma:S^1\to X$ from the unit circle. The map $\gamma$ is a parametrization of this closed [curve](c:curve), and the curve never crosses itself.
examples: The unit circle in $\mathbb R^2$.
The boundary of a triangle or a square in the plane.
A knot in $\mathbb R^3$ is a Jordan curve in space.
Non-example: the figure eight in the plane is not a Jordan curve, because it crosses itself at one point.

steps: Take a Jordan curve, the image of an injection $\gamma:S^1\to X$.
Compose $\gamma$ with the quotient map $[0,1]\to S^1$ to get a continuous path with equal end points.
This path is a closed curve in $X$.
The Jordan case adds that $\gamma$ is injective, so the curve never crosses itself.
links.why: A Jordan curve is a closed curve with no self-crossing, which is what plane theorems on curves need.

reminder: The Lebesgue integral of a nonnegative measurable function is the supremum of the integrals of the simple functions below it.
definition: For a [measure](c:measure) $\mu$ on $X$ and a nonnegative [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $f$, the integral $\int f\,d\mu$ is the supremum of $\sum_ia_i\mu(A_i)$ over simple functions $\sum_ia_i\mathbf 1_{A_i}\le f$. For a general $f$, set $\int f\,d\mu=\int f^+d\mu-\int f^-d\mu$ when this difference makes sense.
examples: For counting measure on $\mathbb N$, $\int f\,d\mu=\sum_nf(n)$.
For Lebesgue measure, $\int\mathbf 1_{\mathbb Q}\,dx=0$, although this function has no Riemann integral.
Non-example: $f(x)=\sin(x)/x$ on $\mathbb R$ has no Lebesgue integral, because $\int f^+$ and $\int f^-$ are both infinite, although the improper Riemann integral exists.

steps: Take a Riemann integrable function $f$ on $[a,b]$.
Then $f$ is bounded and continuous almost everywhere, so $f$ is measurable.
Upper and lower Darboux sums are integrals of step functions, and step functions are simple functions.
So the Lebesgue integral of $f$ exists and equals the Riemann integral.
links.why: The Lebesgue integral keeps every Riemann value and also integrates many more functions.

reminder: The Legendre symbol $(a/p)$ is $1$, $-1$ or $0$ as $a$ is a nonzero square, a non-square or zero modulo $p$.
definition: For an odd [prime number](c:prime-number) $p$ and an integer $a$, the Legendre symbol $\left(\frac ap\right)$ is $1$ if $a$ is a nonzero [quadratic residue](c:quadratic-residue) modulo $p$, $-1$ if $a$ is a non-residue, and $0$ if $p$ divides $a$. By Euler's criterion, $\left(\frac ap\right)\equiv a^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p$.
examples: Modulo $7$ the nonzero squares are $1,2,4$, so $(2/7)=1$ and $(3/7)=-1$.
$(7/7)=0$, and $(ab/p)=(a/p)(b/p)$ for all $a,b$.
Non-example: $(2/15)=1$ is a Jacobi symbol, not a Legendre symbol, because $15$ is not prime and $2$ is not a square modulo $15$.

steps: Take an odd positive integer $n=p_1\cdots p_k$ with prime factors $p_i$.
The Jacobi symbol $(a/n)$ is the product of the Legendre symbols $(a/p_i)$.
When $n$ is prime, the product has one factor.
So the Legendre symbol is the Jacobi symbol with a prime bottom entry.
links.why: Results on the Jacobi symbol, such as reciprocity, restrict to Legendre symbols when the modulus is prime.

reminder: A modular form is a holomorphic function on the upper half-plane with a weight-$k$ transformation law under a congruence subgroup.
definition: Let $\Gamma\subseteq SL_2(\mathbb Z)$ be a congruence subgroup and $k$ an integer. A modular form of weight $k$ for $\Gamma$ is a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) $f$ on the upper half-plane $\mathbb H$ with $f(\gamma z)=(cz+d)^kf(z)$ for every $\gamma=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ in $\Gamma$, and $f$ is holomorphic at every cusp. Here the [group action](c:group-action) of $\Gamma$ on $\mathbb H$ is $\gamma z=\frac{az+b}{cz+d}$.
examples: The Eisenstein series $G_k(z)=\sum_{(m,n)\ne(0,0)}(mz+n)^{-k}$, for even $k\ge4$, has weight $k$ for $SL_2(\mathbb Z)$.
The discriminant $\Delta(z)=q\prod_{n\ge1}(1-q^n)^{24}$, with $q=e^{2\pi iz}$, has weight $12$ for $SL_2(\mathbb Z)$.
Non-example: the $j$-function is invariant under $SL_2(\mathbb Z)$ but has a pole at the cusp $i\infty$, so it is not a modular form.

steps: Take a cusp form $f$ of weight $k$ for $\Gamma$.
It is holomorphic on $\mathbb H$ and satisfies the weight-$k$ law under $\Gamma$.
It is also holomorphic at every cusp, and it vanishes there.
So $f$ meets every condition of a modular form, and cusp forms add the vanishing at the cusps.
links.why: Modular forms contain the cusp forms as the subspace that vanishes at the cusps.

steps: Take the Eisenstein series $G_k$ for even $k\ge4$.
The sum converges absolutely, so $G_k$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb H$.
The map $z\mapsto\gamma z$ permutes the lattice terms, which gives the weight-$k$ law.
At the cusp $i\infty$ the value tends to $2\zeta(k)$, which is finite, so $G_k$ is a modular form.
links.why: Eisenstein series are the first explicit modular forms, and they show that nonzero forms exist.

reminder: A module is an abelian group with scalar multiplication by a ring that obeys the usual vector space laws.
definition: A module over a [ring](c:ring) $R$ with identity is an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) $(M,+)$ with a map $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, such that $r(m+n)=rm+rn$, $(r+s)m=rm+sm$, $(rs)m=r(sm)$ and $1m=m$ for all $r,s\in R$ and $m,n\in M$.
examples: Every vector space over a field $K$ is a module over $K$.
Every abelian group $A$ is a module over $\mathbb Z$, with $n\cdot a=a+\dots+a$ ($n$ times).
A ring $R$ is a module over itself, and its left ideals are its submodules.
Non-example: the group $\mathbb Z/2$ with $r\cdot m=0$ for all $r\in\mathbb Z$ is not a module, because $1\cdot m=m$ fails.

steps: Take a field $K$ and a vector space $V$ over $K$.
A field is a ring, and $V$ is an abelian group under addition.
Scalar multiplication on $V$ satisfies the four module laws.
So $V$ is a module over the ring $K$, and a module over a general ring may lack a basis.
links.why: Modules keep the vector space laws but allow scalars without inverses, so bases can fail to exist.

steps: Take an abelian group $A$ and the ring $\mathbb Z$.
Define $n\cdot a$ as $a+\dots+a$ with $n$ terms, and $(-n)\cdot a$ as $-(n\cdot a)$.
These integer multiples satisfy the four module laws.
So $A$ is a $\mathbb Z$-module, and this structure is the only one on $A$.
links.why: Every fact about modules over a general ring specializes to abelian groups by taking the ring $\mathbb Z$.

reminder: A monotone sequence never decreases or never increases.
definition: A [sequence](c:sequence) $(a_n)$ in a [totally ordered](c:total-order) set is monotone when $a_n\le a_{n+1}$ for all $n$ (non-decreasing) or $a_n\ge a_{n+1}$ for all $n$ (non-increasing). It is strictly monotone when these inequalities are strict.
examples: The sequence $a_n=1/n$ is decreasing, so it is monotone.
The sequence $a_n=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ is non-decreasing but not strictly increasing.
Non-example: $a_n=(-1)^n$ is not monotone, because it goes up and down.

steps: A function $f$ between ordered sets is monotone when $x\le y$ implies $f(x)\le f(y)$.
A sequence is a function $n\mapsto a_n$ on the ordered set $\mathbb N$.
For $n\le m$, the condition $a_n\le a_{n+1}$ for all $n$ gives $a_n\le a_m$ by induction.
So a non-decreasing sequence is a monotone function on $\mathbb N$, and the non-increasing case reverses the order.
links.why: A monotone sequence is a monotone function on the natural numbers, so monotone-function results apply to it.

reminder: Peano arithmetic is the first-order theory of the natural numbers with zero, successor, addition, multiplication and induction.
definition: Peano arithmetic is the theory in [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic) with symbols $0,S,+,\cdot$ whose axioms say $Sx\ne0$, $Sx=Sy\to x=y$, $x+0=x$, $x+Sy=S(x+y)$, $x\cdot0=0$ and $x\cdot Sy=x\cdot y+x$. It also has one induction axiom for each formula $\varphi$: if $\varphi(0)$ and $\forall x\,(\varphi(x)\to\varphi(Sx))$ hold, then $\forall x\,\varphi(x)$. Its standard model is the [natural numbers](c:natural-number).
examples: The natural numbers with the usual successor, sum and product are a model.
Peano arithmetic proves $x+y=y+x$ by induction on $y$.
Non-example: Robinson arithmetic has the same symbols but no induction schema, so it is a weaker theory.

steps: A first-order theory is a set of sentences in a first-order language.
Take the language with symbols $0,S,+,\cdot$.
Collect the successor, addition and multiplication axioms and the induction schema as sentences.
This set of sentences is a first-order theory, so Peano arithmetic is a special case.
links.why: General facts about first-order theories, such as the compactness theorem, apply to Peano arithmetic.

reminder: The product topology is the coarsest topology on a product that makes every projection continuous.
definition: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be [topological spaces](c:topological-space). The product topology on the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product) $\prod_iX_i$ has as a base the sets $\prod_iU_i$ with $U_i$ open in $X_i$ and $U_i=X_i$ for all but finitely many $i$. It is the coarsest topology that makes every projection $\pi_i$ continuous.
examples: On $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$ it is the usual topology of the plane, with open rectangles as a base.
On $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$, with $\{0,1\}$ discrete, it gives the Cantor space.
A net converges in the product topology exactly when it converges in every coordinate.
Non-example: the box topology on $\prod_{n\in\mathbb N}\mathbb R$ allows $U_n\ne\mathbb R$ for infinitely many $n$, so it is strictly finer and is not the product topology.

reminder: A root of a polynomial is a value at which the polynomial equals zero.
definition: A root of a [polynomial](c:polynomial) $p$ with coefficients in a ring $R$ is an element $r$ of $R$, or of a larger ring, with $p(r)=0$. Over a field, $r$ is a root exactly when $x-r$ divides $p$.
examples: The numbers $2$ and $-2$ are roots of $x^2-4$.
The number $1$ is a root of $(x-1)^2$, with multiplicity $2$.
Non-example: $x^2+1$ has no root in $\mathbb R$, because $x^2+1\ge1$ for every real $x$.

reminder: A sheaf is a presheaf whose compatible local sections glue to a unique global section.
definition: A sheaf on a topological space $X$ is a [presheaf](c:presheaf) $F$ such that, for every [open cover](c:open-cover) $\{U_i\}$ of an open set $U$ and all sections $s_i\in F(U_i)$ that agree on overlaps, there is exactly one $s\in F(U)$ with $s|_{U_i}=s_i$ for all $i$. On a site, the same condition holds with covering families in place of open covers.
examples: The continuous real-valued functions on the open sets of $X$.
The smooth sections of a vector bundle over a manifold.

Non-example: the presheaf of constant real functions fails to glue, because the values $0$ and $1$ on two disjoint open sets agree on the empty overlap but come from no constant function on the union.

steps: Take a sheaf $F$ on a space $X$.
It gives a set $F(U)$ for each open set $U$, with restriction maps for inclusions.
These data, with the composition laws, form a presheaf.
A sheaf adds one condition: compatible local sections glue uniquely.
links.why: Every sheaf is a presheaf, so presheaf constructions apply to it, and the gluing condition is the extra property.

reminder: A sphere is the set of points at a fixed distance from a centre.
definition: In a [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$, the sphere of radius $r>0$ about $c$ is $\{x\in X:d(x,c)=r\}$. The $n$-sphere $S^n$ is the unit sphere about the origin in [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb R^{n+1}$.
examples: $S^1$ is the unit circle in $\mathbb R^2$, and $S^2$ is the surface of the unit ball in $\mathbb R^3$.
In $\mathbb R$, the sphere of radius $1$ about $0$ is the two-point set $\{-1,1\}=S^0$.
Non-example: the closed ball $\{x:|x|\le1\}$ is not a sphere, because it contains points at distance less than $1$.

steps: Take $n=1$ in the definition of $S^n$.
The sphere $S^1$ is the set of points $(x,y)$ of $\mathbb R^2$ with $x^2+y^2=1$.
These are the points at distance $1$ from the origin of the plane.
That set is the unit circle, so the circle is the sphere in dimension one.
links.why: The circle is the first sphere, so sphere results in dimension one are results about circles.

steps: Take $n=2$ in the definition of $S^n$.
The sphere $S^2$ is the set of points $(x,y,z)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ with $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$.
These are the points at distance $1$ from the origin of space.
That set is the surface of the unit ball, which is the 2-sphere.
links.why: The 2-sphere is the sphere in dimension two, and general sphere results apply to it.

reminder: The sumset of two sets contains every sum of one element from each set.
definition: For [subsets](c:subset) $A$ and $B$ of an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) $G$, the sumset is $A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,\,b\in B\}$. Some authors call it the Minkowski sum.
examples: Non-example: $\{0,1\}+\{0,2\}$ is not the union $\{0,1\}\cup\{0,2\}$, because $3=1+2$ lies in the sum but in neither set.

reminder: A weak homotopy equivalence is a continuous map that induces isomorphisms on all homotopy groups.
definition: A [continuous map](c:continuous-function) $f:X\to Y$ is a weak homotopy equivalence when it induces a bijection on path components and, for every basepoint $x\in X$ and every $n\ge1$, an isomorphism $\pi_n(X,x)\to\pi_n(Y,f(x))$ of [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group).
examples: Every homotopy equivalence is a weak homotopy equivalence.
A CW approximation $\Gamma X\to X$ of any space $X$ is a weak homotopy equivalence.
Non-example: the map $S^1\to\ast$ to a point is not one, because $\pi_1(S^1)=\mathbb Z$ but $\pi_1(\ast)$ is trivial.

steps: Take a homotopy equivalence $f:X\to Y$ with homotopy inverse $g$.
Homotopic maps induce equal maps on homotopy groups, so $f_*$ and $g_*$ are inverse isomorphisms.
This holds at every basepoint and in every degree $n$.
So $f$ is a weak homotopy equivalence, and the converse holds between CW complexes.
links.why: Weak equivalences are the maps that algebraic topology cannot tell apart from homotopy equivalences.

reminder: An abelian group is a group whose operation is commutative.
definition: An abelian group is a [group](c:group) $(G,\cdot)$ with $ab=ba$ for all $a,b\in G$. Authors often write the operation as $+$, the identity as $0$ and the inverse of $a$ as $-a$.
examples: The integers, rationals and reals under addition.
The integers modulo $n$ under addition, and every vector space under vector addition.
Non-example: the symmetric group $S_3$ is not abelian, because $(12)(13)\ne(13)(12)$.

steps: Take an abelian group $G$.
Forget commutativity and keep the operation, the identity and the inverses.
These data form a group.
The abelian case adds the single condition $ab=ba$.
links.why: Every group theorem holds for abelian groups, and commutativity gives extra tools such as quotients by every subgroup.

steps: Take a cyclic group $G$ generated by one element $g$.
Every element of $G$ has the form $g^n$.
Then $g^mg^n=g^{m+n}=g^ng^m$ for all $m,n$.
So $G$ is abelian, and abelian groups need not have one generator.
links.why: Cyclic groups are the simplest abelian groups, and the structure theorems build every finite abelian group from them.

reminder: An antichain is a subset of a partially ordered set in which no two distinct elements are comparable.
definition: In a [partially ordered set](c:partial-order) $(P,\le)$, a [subset](c:subset) $A\subseteq P$ is an antichain when, for all distinct $a,b\in A$, neither $a\le b$ nor $b\le a$ holds. The empty set and every one-element subset are antichains.
examples: In the subsets of $\{1,2,3\}$ ordered by inclusion, the three singletons form an antichain.
In $\mathbb N$ ordered by divisibility, the set of prime numbers is an antichain.
Non-example: in a total order, no two-element set is an antichain, because any two elements are comparable.

reminder: Area measures the two-dimensional size of a plane region in square units.
definition: The area of a measurable region $R\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is its two-dimensional Lebesgue measure, so a rectangle with sides $a$ and $b$ has area $ab$. Area is additive on disjoint regions and unchanged by rigid motions of [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space). For a smooth surface $r(u,v)$ in $\mathbb R^3$ it is $\iint\|r_u\times r_v\|\,du\,dv$.
examples: A triangle with base $b$ and height $h$ has area $bh/2$.
The unit disc has area $\pi$.
Non-example: the perimeter of a square is a length, not an area, because doubling the sides doubles the perimeter but multiplies the area by $4$.

steps: Take the plane $\mathbb R^2$ with its Borel sets.
Give each rectangle $[a,b]\times[c,d]$ the value $(b-a)(d-c)$.
This assignment extends to a unique countably additive measure on the Borel sets of the plane, the Lebesgue measure.
The area of a region is the value of this measure, so area is Lebesgue measure in dimension two.
links.why: Area inherits additivity, limits and integration from measure theory.

reminder: A bounded operator is a linear map that sends bounded sets to bounded sets.
definition: A [linear map](c:linear-map) $T:X\to Y$ between [normed spaces](c:normed-space) is bounded when $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for some constant $C$ and all $x$, which is equivalent to being continuous. The same bounded-sets definition applies to a map between [topological vector spaces](c:topological-vector-space), where a set is bounded when each neighbourhood of $0$ absorbs it.
examples: Multiplication by a matrix, as a map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$.
The shift $(x_1,x_2,\dots)\mapsto(0,x_1,x_2,\dots)$ on $\ell^2$, which has norm $1$.
Non-example: differentiation $d/dx$ on $C^1[0,1]$ with the supremum norm is unbounded, because $\sin(nx)$ has norm at most $1$ but its derivative has norm $n$.

steps: A linear map $T$ satisfies $T(x+y)=Tx+Ty$ and $T(ax)=aTx$.
Take a linear map between normed spaces.
The bounded case adds one condition: $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for some constant $C$.
This condition makes $T$ continuous, which a general linear map need not be.
links.why: Boundedness turns an algebraic map into one that analysis can use, since it gives continuity.

steps: Take a compact operator $T:X\to Y$ between normed spaces.
By definition $T$ maps bounded sets to sets with compact closure.
A compact set is bounded, so $T$ maps bounded sets to bounded sets.
So $T$ is a bounded operator, and the compact case adds relative compactness of the image.
links.why: Every theorem on bounded operators applies to compact operators, which are the nicest bounded ones.

reminder: The character of a representation sends each group element to the trace of its action.
definition: Let $\rho:G\to GL(V)$ be a finite-dimensional [representation](c:group-representation) of a group $G$ on a vector space $V$. Its character is the function $\chi_\rho:G\to K$ with $\chi_\rho(g)=\operatorname{tr}\rho(g)$, the [trace](c:trace-of-a-matrix) of the matrix of $\rho(g)$.
examples: The trivial representation of dimension $d$ has the constant character $d$, and every character has $\chi(e)=\dim V$.
The sign representation of $S_n$ has the character $g\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(g)$.
Non-example: on $S_3$, the function equal to $1$ at $(12)$ and $0$ elsewhere is not a character, because $(12)$ and $(13)$ are conjugate but get different values.

reminder: The characteristic function of a random variable $X$ sends $t$ to the expected value of $e^{itX}$.
definition: For a real [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$, the characteristic function is $\varphi_X(t)=\mathbb E[e^{itX}]$ for $t\in\mathbb R$, where $\mathbb E$ is the [expected value](c:expected-value). It is the [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) of the distribution of $X$, and it determines this distribution.
examples: For a standard normal variable, $\varphi_X(t)=e^{-t^2/2}$.
For a Bernoulli variable with $P(X=1)=p$, $\varphi_X(t)=1-p+pe^{it}$.
Non-example: the moment generating function $\mathbb E[e^{tX}]$ is a different function, and it is infinite for every $t\ne0$ for a Cauchy variable, while $\varphi_X$ always exists.

steps: Take the law $\mu_X$ of $X$, a probability measure on $\mathbb R$.
By the change of variables formula, $\mathbb E[e^{itX}]=\int e^{itx}\,d\mu_X(x)$.
This integral is the Fourier transform of $\mu_X$, up to the sign in the exponent.
So the characteristic function is the Fourier transform of a probability measure.
links.why: Fourier tools, such as inversion and continuity, apply to characteristic functions and give limit theorems.

reminder: A clique is a set of vertices of a graph in which every two vertices are adjacent.
definition: In a [graph](c:graph) $G=(V,E)$, a clique is a subset $K\subseteq V$ such that $\{u,v\}\in E$ for all distinct $u,v\in K$. A clique with $k$ vertices is a $k$-clique, and the largest size of a clique is the clique number of $G$.
examples: Every single vertex, and every edge with its two end points, is a clique.
Every triangle is a 3-clique, and in the complete graph $K_n$ the whole vertex set is a clique.
Non-example: in the path $a-b-c$ the set $\{a,b,c\}$ is not a clique, because $a$ and $c$ are not adjacent.

reminder: A compact Hausdorff space has a finite subcover for every open cover, and it separates distinct points by disjoint open sets.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is compact Hausdorff when it is [compact](c:compact-space), so every open cover has a finite subcover, and [Hausdorff](c:hausdorff-space), so distinct points have disjoint open neighbourhoods.
examples: The interval $[0,1]$, and every closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R^n$.
The spheres $S^n$ and the Cantor set.
Non-example: $\mathbb R$ is Hausdorff but not compact, and a two-point space with the indiscrete topology is compact but not Hausdorff.

steps: Take a compact Hausdorff space $X$.
Forget the Hausdorff condition and keep the topology.
Every open cover of $X$ still has a finite subcover, so $X$ is compact.
The compact Hausdorff case adds that distinct points have disjoint open neighbourhoods.
links.why: Compact Hausdorff spaces have all compactness results, plus closed compact sets and uniqueness of limits.

steps: Take a compact Hausdorff space $X$.
Forget the compactness condition and keep the topology.
Distinct points of $X$ still have disjoint open neighbourhoods, so $X$ is Hausdorff.
The compact Hausdorff case adds that every open cover has a finite subcover.
links.why: Compact Hausdorff spaces have all Hausdorff results, such as unique limits of sequences and nets.

reminder: A continuously differentiable map is differentiable, and its derivative depends continuously on the point.
definition: A map $f:U\to F$ from an open subset $U$ of a normed space $E$ to a normed space $F$ is continuously differentiable, or of class $C^1$, when it is [differentiable](c:differentiation) at every point of $U$ and $x\mapsto Df(x)$ is a [continuous](c:continuous-function) map from $U$ to the space of [bounded operators](c:bounded-operator) $E\to F$ with the operator norm.
examples: Every polynomial map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$.
A map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is of class $C^1$ exactly when all its partial derivatives exist and are continuous.
Non-example: $f(x)=x^2\sin(1/x)$ with $f(0)=0$ is differentiable on $\mathbb R$, but $f'$ is not continuous at $0$.

steps: A differentiable map $f:U\to F$ has a derivative $Df(x)$ at every point $x$ of $U$.
Take a continuously differentiable map and keep these derivatives.
The map is differentiable at each point of $U$.
The $C^1$ case adds that $x\mapsto Df(x)$ is continuous.
links.why: Continuity of the derivative is the condition that inverse and implicit function theorems need.

steps: Take a smooth function $f$ on an open set $U$.
Smooth means that $f$ has derivatives of all orders, so $f$ is differentiable and $Df$ is differentiable.
A differentiable map is continuous, so $Df$ is continuous.
So $f$ is of class $C^1$.
links.why: Every smooth function meets the $C^1$ hypothesis, so $C^1$ theorems apply to it.

reminder: Curvature measures how far a curve, surface or Riemannian manifold bends away from being flat.
definition: For a plane curve $\gamma(s)$ parametrized by arc length, the curvature is $\kappa(s)=\|\gamma''(s)\|$, the rate at which the unit tangent turns. For a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold), the curvature is the Riemann tensor $R$, built from second [derivatives](c:derivative) of the metric, and it vanishes exactly when the manifold is locally flat.
examples: A circle of radius $r$ has curvature $1/r$ at every point, and a straight line has curvature $0$.
A sphere of radius $r$ has Gaussian curvature $1/r^2$.
Non-example: the length of a curve is not its curvature, because a long straight line has large length and curvature $0$.

steps: Take a Riemannian manifold with curvature tensor $R$.
Choose a point $p$ and orthonormal tangent vectors $u,v$ at $p$.
Evaluate $R$ on the four vectors $u,v,v,u$ to get one number.
This number is the sectional curvature of the plane spanned by $u,v$, and all such numbers determine $R$.
links.why: Sectional curvature turns the curvature tensor into one number per plane, which is easier to bound and compare.

steps: Take the curvature tensor $R$ at a point $p$.
Fix a unit tangent vector $v$ and extend it to an orthonormal basis $v,e_2,\dots,e_n$.
Add the sectional curvatures $K(v,e_i)$ for $i=2,\dots,n$.
This sum is the Ricci curvature $\operatorname{Ric}(v,v)$, a trace of $R$.
links.why: Ricci curvature keeps part of the information in $R$, and it is the quantity that Einstein's equations use.

reminder: A direct sum of modules is the module of families with finitely many nonzero entries and componentwise operations.
definition: The direct sum $\bigoplus_{i\in I}M_i$ of [modules](c:module) $M_i$ over a ring $R$ is the set of families $(m_i)_{i\in I}$ in the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product) $\prod_iM_i$ with $m_i=0$ for all but finitely many $i$, with addition and scalar multiplication taken componentwise. For finitely many summands it equals the product, so $V\oplus W$ is the set of pairs $(v,w)$.
examples: $\mathbb R^2=\mathbb R\oplus\mathbb R$, and $\mathbb Z/2\oplus\mathbb Z/3\cong\mathbb Z/6$.
$\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb N}\mathbb R$ is the space of real sequences with finitely many nonzero terms.
Non-example: $\prod_{n\in\mathbb N}\mathbb R$, the space of all real sequences, is not the direct sum, because it contains $(1,1,1,\dots)$ with infinitely many nonzero entries.

steps: A coproduct of the $M_i$ is an object $S$ with maps $\iota_i:M_i\to S$ through which maps out of $S$ factor uniquely.
Take $S=\bigoplus_iM_i$ and let $\iota_i$ put $m$ in coordinate $i$.
Given linear maps $f_i:M_i\to N$, define $f(m)=\sum_if_i(m_i)$, a finite sum.
This $f$ is the unique linear map with $f\iota_i=f_i$, so the direct sum is the coproduct of modules.
links.why: The universal property of the coproduct explains why linear maps out of a direct sum are families of maps.

reminder: In a distributive lattice, meet distributes over join.
definition: A [lattice](c:lattice) $(L,\wedge,\vee)$ is distributive when $a\wedge(b\vee c)=(a\wedge b)\vee(a\wedge c)$ for all $a,b,c\in L$. This law is equivalent to the dual law $a\vee(b\wedge c)=(a\vee b)\wedge(a\vee c)$.
examples: The subsets of a set, ordered by inclusion, with $\cap$ as meet and $\cup$ as join.
Every total order, with the minimum as meet and the maximum as join.
Non-example: the diamond lattice with bottom $0$, top $1$ and three incomparable middle elements $a,b,c$ is not distributive, because $a\wedge(b\vee c)=a$ but $(a\wedge b)\vee(a\wedge c)=0$.

steps: Take a distributive lattice $(L,\wedge,\vee)$.
Forget the distributive law and keep the meet and the join.
These operations form a lattice.
The distributive case adds the law $a\wedge(b\vee c)=(a\wedge b)\vee(a\wedge c)$.
links.why: Distributive lattices have every lattice result, plus unique complements and representation by sets.

steps: Take a Boolean algebra $B$, a lattice with top, bottom and complements.
Its meet and join satisfy the lattice axioms.
The distributive law is part of the axioms of a Boolean algebra.
So $B$ is a distributive lattice, and the Boolean case adds bounds and complements.
links.why: Boolean algebras are the distributive lattices that also have complements.

reminder: A finite-dimensional vector space has a basis with finitely many vectors.
definition: A [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ is finite-dimensional when it has a finite [basis](c:basis), that is, finitely many vectors $v_1,\dots,v_n$ that are linearly independent and span $V$. The number $n$ does not depend on the basis, and it is the dimension $\dim V$.
examples: The space $K^n$ has dimension $n$.
The polynomials of degree at most $d$ form a space of dimension $d+1$.
Non-example: the space of all real polynomials is not finite-dimensional, because a finite set of polynomials has bounded degree and cannot span.

steps: A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication that obey the vector space laws.
Take a finite-dimensional space and keep these operations.
These data form a vector space.
The finite-dimensional case adds that finitely many vectors span the space.
links.why: A finite-dimensional space has coordinates, so matrices and determinants apply to it.

reminder: The intersection form of a closed oriented $4k$-manifold pairs two middle-dimensional classes by counting how their cycles meet.
definition: Let $M$ be a closed [oriented](c:orientation-of-a-manifold) manifold of dimension $4k$. Its intersection form is the [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) on $H_{2k}(M;\mathbb Z)$ modulo torsion that sends two classes to the signed count of intersection points of transverse representing cycles, and by Poincaré duality it is symmetric and unimodular. Here $H_{2k}$ is the middle [homology](c:homology).
examples: For the complex projective plane $\mathbb{CP}^2$, $H_2=\mathbb Z$ and the form is the $1\times1$ matrix $(1)$.
For $S^2\times S^2$ the form is the matrix with rows $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$.
Non-example: on the torus $T^2$, of dimension $2$, the intersection pairing on $H_1$ is skew-symmetric, so it is not a symmetric intersection form of dimension $4k$.

steps: A bilinear form on a free abelian group is a map that is additive in each argument.
The intersection count is additive in each cycle, because intersections add under sums of cycles.
Poincaré duality makes the pairing symmetric and unimodular when the dimension is $4k$.
So the intersection form is a symmetric, unimodular bilinear form over $\mathbb Z$.
links.why: Algebra of bilinear forms, such as signature and rank, becomes an invariant of the manifold.

reminder: A linear functional is a linear map from a vector space to its field of scalars.
definition: A linear functional on a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over a field $K$ is a [linear map](c:linear-map) $\varphi:V\to K$, so $\varphi(au+bv)=a\varphi(u)+b\varphi(v)$ for all scalars $a,b$ and vectors $u,v$.
examples: The coordinate map $x\mapsto x_i$ on $K^n$.
The evaluation $f\mapsto f(0)$ on the space of polynomials, and $f\mapsto\int_0^1f(x)\,dx$ on $C[0,1]$.
Non-example: $x\mapsto x+1$ on $\mathbb R$ is not a linear functional, because it sends $0$ to $1$.

steps: A linear map $T:V\to W$ is additive and respects scalar multiples.
Choose $W=K$, the field of scalars viewed as a one-dimensional vector space.
The linear maps $V\to K$ are exactly the linear functionals.
So the functional case adds the condition that the target is the scalar field.
links.why: Scalar values let us add and compare functionals and define the dual space with them.

reminder: A locally convex space is a topological vector space with a base of convex neighbourhoods of zero.
definition: A [topological vector space](c:topological-vector-space) $X$ is locally convex when every neighbourhood of $0$ contains a [convex](c:convex-set) neighbourhood of $0$. Equivalently, its topology comes from a family of seminorms $(p_i)$, with basic neighbourhoods $\{x:p_{i_1}(x)<\varepsilon,\dots,p_{i_n}(x)<\varepsilon\}$.
examples: Every normed space, where the norm is the only seminorm.
The space $C(\mathbb R)$ of continuous functions with the seminorms $\sup_{[-n,n]}|f|$, and the Schwartz space.
Non-example: $L^p[0,1]$ for $0<p<1$ is a topological vector space, but its only open convex sets are the empty set and the whole space, so it is not locally convex.

steps: A topological vector space is a vector space with a topology that makes addition and scalar multiplication continuous.
Take a locally convex space and keep this structure.
It is a topological vector space.
The locally convex case adds that convex neighbourhoods of $0$ form a base.
links.why: Convex neighbourhoods let the Hahn-Banach separation theorems work in the space.

steps: Take a normed space $(X,\|\cdot\|)$.
The open balls $\{x:\|x\|<r\}$ form a base of neighbourhoods of $0$.
Each ball is convex, by the triangle inequality and the homogeneity of the norm.
So $X$ is locally convex, and the norm is one seminorm that defines its topology.
links.why: Locally convex spaces allow many seminorms, which covers function spaces that no single norm describes.

reminder: The logarithm is the inverse of the exponential function: $\log x$ is the number $y$ with $e^y=x$.
definition: The natural logarithm $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse of the [exponential function](c:exponential-function) $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$, so $\log x=y$ exactly when $e^y=x$. It turns products into sums, $\log(xy)=\log x+\log y$, and the logarithm to a base $b>0$ with $b\ne1$ is $\log_bx=\log x/\log b$.
examples: $\log1=0$ and $\log e=1$.
$\log_28=3$, because $2^3=8$, and $\log(x^k)=k\log x$.
Non-example: $\log0$ and $\log(-1)$ are not real numbers, because $e^y>0$ for every real $y$.

reminder: The power set of a set is the set of all its subsets.
definition: The power set $\mathcal P(S)$ of a [set](c:set) $S$ is the set $\{A:A\subseteq S\}$ of all [subsets](c:subset) of $S$, including $\emptyset$ and $S$. If $S$ has $n$ elements, then $\mathcal P(S)$ has $2^n$ elements.
examples: $\mathcal P(\{a,b\})=\{\emptyset,\{a\},\{b\},\{a,b\}\}$.
$\mathcal P(\emptyset)=\{\emptyset\}$, a set with exactly one element.
Non-example: $a$ is not an element of $\mathcal P(\{a,b\})$, because the elements of a power set are subsets and $a$ is a point.

reminder: A projective variety is the common zero set of homogeneous polynomials in projective space, usually irreducible.
definition: A projective variety over a field $k$ is a set $V=\{F_1=\dots=F_r=0\}$ in [projective space](c:projective-space) $\mathbb P^n_k$, where the $F_j$ are homogeneous [polynomials](c:polynomial) in $x_0,\dots,x_n$. Usually one also requires $V$ to be irreducible, so that it is an [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety).
examples: A line or a plane in $\mathbb P^n$, cut out by linear equations.
The conic $x^2+y^2=z^2$ in $\mathbb P^2$, and the Fermat cubic $x^3+y^3+z^3=0$.
Non-example: the equation $x+y^2=1$ is not homogeneous, so it defines no subset of $\mathbb P^2$, because $[x:y:z]$ and $[2x:2y:2z]$ give different values.

steps: Cover $\mathbb P^n$ by the affine charts $x_i\ne0$.
In each chart, $V$ is the zero set of the polynomials $F_j$ with $x_i=1$.
So affine algebraic varieties that glue together cover $V$.
Hence $V$ is an algebraic variety, and the projective case adds that $V$ is closed in projective space.
links.why: Projective varieties are the complete varieties of classical geometry, where intersection theory behaves well.

reminder: The sectional curvature of a 2-plane is the Gaussian curvature of the surface that geodesics in that plane sweep out.
definition: Let $M$ be a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold), $p\in M$ and $\sigma$ a 2-plane in the tangent space $T_pM$. The sectional curvature $K(\sigma)$ is the [Gaussian curvature](c:gaussian-curvature) at $p$ of the surface swept out by the geodesics through $p$ tangent to $\sigma$. It equals $\langle R(u,v)v,u\rangle$ for orthonormal $u,v$ spanning $\sigma$, up to the sign convention for the [curvature](c:curvature) tensor $R$.
examples: The unit sphere $S^n$ has $K=1$ on every plane.
Euclidean space has $K=0$ on every plane, and hyperbolic space has $K=-1$.
Non-example: Ricci curvature is not sectional curvature, because it sums sectional curvatures over a basis and depends on one vector, not on a plane.

steps: Take a surface $S$ with its Riemannian metric.
At each point $p$ the tangent space $T_pS$ is the only 2-plane.
The geodesics tangent to this plane sweep out $S$ itself near $p$.
So $K(T_pS)$ is the Gaussian curvature of $S$ at $p$.
links.why: Sectional curvature carries the Gaussian curvature of surfaces to every dimension.

steps: The Riemann tensor $R$ gives the number $\langle R(u,v)v,u\rangle$ for each pair of vectors $u,v$.
For orthonormal $u,v$, this number depends only on the plane they span.
So sectional curvature restricts $R$ to planes.
The sectional curvatures at $p$ determine $R$ at $p$ completely.
links.why: Authors state curvature bounds, such as $K\le0$, with sectional curvature, and these bounds control the whole tensor.

reminder: A contractible space can be continuously shrunk to a point.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is contractible when its identity map is [homotopic](c:homotopy) to a constant map. Equivalently, the map $X\to\ast$ to a point is a homotopy equivalence. It is weakly contractible when all its homotopy groups are trivial.
examples: The space $\mathbb R^n$, the closed disc $D^n$, and every convex subset of $\mathbb R^n$.
A single point, which is the model of a contractible space.
Non-example: the circle $S^1$ is not contractible, because $\pi_1(S^1)=\mathbb Z$ is not trivial.

steps: Take a star-shaped domain $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with centre $c$.
Define $H(x,t)=(1-t)x+tc$ for $x\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$.
Star-shapedness keeps $H(x,t)$ inside $U$, so $H$ is continuous into $U$.
The map $H$ is a homotopy from the identity to the constant map at $c$, so $U$ is contractible.
links.why: Contractibility explains why star-shaped and convex sets have no topology, for example in the Poincaré lemma.

reminder: The convolution of two functions at $x$ is the integral of $f(y)g(x-y)$ over $y$.
definition: For functions $f,g$ on $\mathbb R^n$, the convolution is $(f*g)(x)=\int f(y)g(x-y)\,dy$, at each point where this [integral](c:integral) exists. On $\mathbb Z$ it is the sum $\sum_yf(y)g(x-y)$, and the convolution averages $f$ against translates of the [function](c:function) $g$.
examples: If $f=g=\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}$, then $f*g$ is a triangle function supported on $[0,2]$.
If $X$ and $Y$ are independent with densities $f$ and $g$, then $X+Y$ has density $f*g$.
Non-example: for $f=g=1$ on $\mathbb R$ the convolution is undefined, because $\int1\,dy=\infty$.

reminder: The distribution function of a random variable $X$ gives $P(X\le x)$ for each real $x$.
definition: For a real [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$ with [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $P$, the distribution function is $F_X(x)=P(X\le x)$. It is non-decreasing and right-continuous, with limits $0$ at $-\infty$ and $1$ at $+\infty$, and it determines the law of $X$.
examples: For $X$ uniform on $[0,1]$, $F(x)=x$ on $[0,1]$, with $F=0$ below and $F=1$ above.
For a fair coin coded as $X\in\{0,1\}$, $F$ jumps by $1/2$ at $0$ and at $1$.
Non-example: $G(x)=0$ for $x\le0$ and $G(x)=1$ for $x>0$ is not a distribution function, because it is not right-continuous at $0$.

reminder: An elementary embedding preserves the truth of every first-order formula with parameters.
definition: Let $M$ and $N$ be structures for one language of [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic). A map $j:M\to N$ is an elementary embedding when $M\models\varphi(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ if and only if $N\models\varphi(j(a_1),\dots,j(a_n))$ for every formula $\varphi$ and all $a_i\in M$. Then $M$ is isomorphic to an elementary [substructure](c:substructure) of $N$.
examples: Every isomorphism of structures is an elementary embedding.
The inclusion $(\mathbb Q,<)\to(\mathbb R,<)$ is elementary, because the theory of dense linear orders without end points has quantifier elimination.
Non-example: the inclusion $(\mathbb N,<)\to(\mathbb Z,<)$ is not elementary, because $\exists y\,(y<0)$ is false in $\mathbb N$ and true in $\mathbb Z$.

steps: Take structures $M\subseteq N$ where $M$ is an elementary substructure of $N$.
By definition $M$ and $N$ satisfy the same formulas with parameters from $M$.
So the inclusion $M\to N$ preserves the truth of every such formula.
Hence the inclusion is an elementary embedding, and every elementary embedding is of this kind up to isomorphism.
links.why: Elementary embeddings let one move between a structure and a larger one without changing its first-order truths.

reminder: A family of sets is a collection of subsets of a fixed set, possibly with an index.
definition: A family of sets in a [set](c:set) $X$ is a collection $\mathcal F$ of [subsets](c:subset) of $X$, that is, a subset of the [power set](c:power-set) of $X$, or an indexed family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ with each $A_i\subseteq X$. An indexed family may list the same set under different indices.
examples: The open sets of a topological space.
The edges of a graph, taken as two-element subsets of its vertex set.
The family $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ with $A_n=\{k:k\ge n\}$.
Non-example: $\{1,\{2\}\}$ is not a family of subsets of $\{1,2\}$, because $1$ is an element, not a subset.

steps: Take an open cover $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ of a space $X$.
Each $U_i$ is an open subset of $X$, so $(U_i)$ is an indexed family of subsets.
The cover adds two conditions: every $U_i$ is open and the union of all $U_i$ is $X$.
Forget these conditions and the cover is a family of sets.
links.why: Results on families of sets apply to covers once the open and covering conditions are set aside.

reminder: A finitely generated group has a finite set of elements whose products and inverses give every element.
definition: A [group](c:group) $G$ is finitely generated when some [finite set](c:finite-set) $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_n\}\subseteq G$ has the property that every element of $G$ is a finite product of elements of $S$ and their inverses. Equivalently, $G$ is the smallest subgroup that contains $S$.
examples: The element $1$ generates $\mathbb Z$, and the $n$ unit vectors generate $\mathbb Z^n$.
Every finite group is finitely generated, and so is the free group on two letters $a,b$.
Non-example: $\mathbb Q$ under addition is not finitely generated, because finitely many fractions have a common denominator $d$ and generate only a subgroup of $\frac1d\mathbb Z$.

steps: Take a cyclic group $G$ with generator $g$.
The one-element set $\{g\}$ is finite.
Every element of $G$ is a power $g^n$, so it is a product of copies of $g$ or $g^{-1}$.
So $G$ is finitely generated, and the general case allows any finite number of generators.
links.why: Finitely generated groups extend cyclic groups to any finite list of generators.

steps: Take a finite group $G$.
Let $S=G$, which is a finite set.
Every element $g$ of $G$ lies in $S$, so it is a product of length one.
So $G$ is finitely generated, and infinite groups such as $\mathbb Q$ need not be.
links.why: Finite groups are the easiest finitely generated groups, and infinite examples need new tools.

reminder: The $n$-th Fourier coefficient of a periodic function is its average against $e^{-int}$.
definition: For an integrable function $f$ with period $2\pi$, the $n$-th Fourier coefficient is $\hat f(n)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(t)e^{-int}\,dt$ for $n\in\mathbb Z$, where the [integral](c:integral) is the Lebesgue integral. The [Fourier series](c:fourier-series) of $f$ is $\sum_n\hat f(n)e^{int}$. Replacing $f(t)\,dt$ by a finite measure gives the coefficients of a measure.
examples: For $f(t)=\cos t$, $\hat f(1)=\hat f(-1)=\tfrac12$ and all other coefficients are $0$.
For a constant function $c$, $\hat f(0)=c$ and all other coefficients are $0$.
Non-example: the function $1/|t|$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$ has no Fourier coefficients, because its integral diverges.

steps: The Fourier transform on a locally compact abelian group integrates a function against the characters of the group.
Take the circle group $\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$, whose characters are $t\mapsto e^{int}$ for $n\in\mathbb Z$.
The transform of $f$ at the character $e^{int}$ is $\hat f(n)$, the integral of $f$ against the conjugate character.
So the Fourier coefficients form the Fourier transform on the circle, a function on $\mathbb Z$.
links.why: Fourier coefficients are the discrete case of the Fourier transform, so transform rules carry over.

reminder: A free module has a basis, so every element is a unique combination of basis elements.
definition: A [module](c:module) $M$ over a ring $R$ is free when it has a [basis](c:basis), that is, a subset $B$ such that every $m\in M$ is a unique finite $R$-linear combination of elements of $B$. Equivalently, $M$ is isomorphic to a [direct sum](c:direct-sum) $\bigoplus_{b\in B}R$ of copies of $R$.
examples: The module $R^n$ for any ring $R$.
The polynomial ring $R[x]$ as an $R$-module, with basis $1,x,x^2,\dots$.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z/2$ as a $\mathbb Z$-module is not free, because $2m=0$ for every element $m$, so no element is linearly independent.

steps: Take a free module $M$ over $R$ with basis $B$.
Forget the basis and keep the addition and the scalar multiplication.
These data form a module.
The free case adds the condition that a basis exists.
links.why: Free modules have bases, so they behave like vector spaces and have matrices for their maps.

steps: Take a vector space $V$ over a field $K$, viewed as a $K$-module.
Choose a basis $B$ of $V$, which uses the axiom of choice when $V$ is infinite-dimensional.
Each vector is a unique finite combination of $B$, which is the definition of a basis of a module.
So $V$ is a free $K$-module, and over a general ring a module can lack a basis.
links.why: Free modules are the vector space case, with a ring in place of the field.

steps: Take a free module $F$ with basis $B$, a surjection $g:N\to L$ and a map $f:F\to L$.
For each $b\in B$, choose $n_b\in N$ with $g(n_b)=f(b)$.
Define $h:F\to N$ by $h(b)=n_b$ and extend $h$ linearly.
Then $gh=f$, so $F$ is projective, and the converse fails for some rings.
links.why: A free module is projective, so projective-module results apply to free modules.

reminder: The fundamental group of a space at a point has homotopy classes of loops at that point, composed by concatenation.
definition: For a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ with basepoint $x_0$, the fundamental group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is the set of classes of loops $\gamma:[0,1]\to X$ with $\gamma(0)=\gamma(1)=x_0$, where two loops are the same class when they are [homotopic](c:homotopy) relative to the end points. The product of two classes is the class of the loop that runs the first loop and then the second, and this makes $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ a [group](c:group).
examples: $\pi_1(S^1)\cong\mathbb Z$, where an integer counts how often a loop winds around the circle.
$\pi_1(\mathbb R^n)$ and $\pi_1(S^2)$ are trivial, and $\pi_1(S^1\vee S^1)$ is the free group on two letters.
Non-example: the set of all loops at $x_0$, without identifying homotopic loops, is not a group under concatenation, because concatenation is not associative and loops have no inverses.

steps: The homotopy group $\pi_n(X,x_0)$ is the set of classes of maps $(S^n,\ast)\to(X,x_0)$ up to based homotopy.
Take the case $n=1$ of this definition.
A based map from the circle $S^1$ is a loop at $x_0$.
So $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is the fundamental group, with the loop product as group law.
links.why: The fundamental group is the first homotopy group, and the only one that may be non-abelian.

reminder: A homotopy from $f$ to $g$ is a continuous family of maps that starts at $f$ and ends at $g$.
definition: Let $f,g:X\to Y$ be [continuous maps](c:continuous-function). A homotopy from $f$ to $g$ is a continuous map $H:X\times[0,1]\to Y$ with $H(x,0)=f(x)$ and $H(x,1)=g(x)$ for all $x\in X$, where $[0,1]$ is the unit [interval](c:interval). Then $f$ and $g$ are homotopic, and this is an equivalence relation on maps $X\to Y$.
examples: If $Y=\mathbb R^n$, then $H(x,t)=(1-t)f(x)+tg(x)$ is a homotopy between any two maps $f,g$.
On the closed disc, the identity map is homotopic to the constant map at the centre by $H(x,t)=(1-t)x$.
Non-example: the identity map of $S^1$ and a constant map are not homotopic, because their winding numbers $1$ and $0$ differ.

steps: Take an isotopy $H:X\times[0,1]\to Y$, a family of embeddings that varies continuously in $t$.
The map $H$ is continuous in $(x,t)$.
So $H$ is a homotopy from the first embedding to the last.
A homotopy drops the condition that every $H(\cdot,t)$ is an embedding.
links.why: Homotopy relaxes isotopy, so it is easier to build and still keeps topological invariants.
